title: Immunohistochemical expression of Claudin 1 &Claudin 3 in Radicular cyst, Odontogenic keratocyst, Unicystic ameloblastoma and Conventional ameloblastoma
author: Safa Fathy

steps_raw.instruction: Introduction & Review of Literature

Odontogenic lesions are uniquely derived from the tissues of developing teeth; most of them affect the osseous marrow and cortex of the jaw bones. They are divided into odontogenic cysts and tumors. Odontogenic cysts are cavities lined by odontogenic derived epithelium. They are the most common lesions of the jaw, especially radicular cysts (RC) and odontogenic keratocysts (OKC). While, RC shows an indolent behavior and rarely recurs after surgical removal, the KOT is invasive and destructive. On the other hand, odontogenic tumors are classified according to behavior into benign and malignant, in addition according to origin into epithelial and mesenchymal. The most common benign odontogenic tumor is ameloblastoma. It is a locally aggressive epithelial tumor that shows marked invasion and multiple recurrences after enucleation and curettage. Unicystic ameloblastoma is a less aggressive variant of ameloblastoma, which has a lower recurrence rate (Da Silava, 2008 and Wang et al, 2008).

These lesions have many adverse effects on the jaw bone such as bone resorption that may lead to jaw fracture, looseness of the teeth, recent occlusal problems, delayed tooth eruption, swellings and intraoral bleeding. A number of studies have explored the expression of various immunohistochemical markers for the establishment of differences in the biologic behavior of the odontogenic cysts and tumors. Claudins are recent markers that have been found in tumors derived from cells containing TJs, such as epithelial and endothelial tumors (Soini, 2004, Soini, 2005). However, scarce studies were accomplished to detect their expression in odontogenic lesions. Proper evaluation of the actual localization of claudins in odontogenic lesions might add a lot to our understanding of the role of these proteins in formation, growth potential, behavior and prognosis of these lesions.

The name "Claudin" was derived from the Latin word “claudere,” which means to close, as it was anticipated that these proteins were the main components of the tight junctional barrier (Tsukita and Fursue, 2002). The claudins constitute a protein family of 24 members in mammals, with a molecular mass ranging from 20 to 27 kDa. It is confirmed that they are the main components of tight junctions (TJs). TJs are critical for maintaining normal structure and physiological function of the epithelium and endothelium (Langbein et al, 2003 and Itoh et al, 2003). They serve as a physical barrier to prevent solutes and water from passing freely through the paracellular space between epithelial and endothelial cell sheets, and also play critical roles in maintaining cell polarity and signal transduction (Matter et al, 2003 and Shin et al, 2006). Claudins often show tissue-specific patterns of expression. Claudin-aberrant expression potentially leads to structural and functional damage of TJs, as it is a central component determining the integrity of the TJ (Krause et al, 2008).
Immunohistochemical expression of Claudin-3:

Claudin-3 is widely expressed in a variety of normal and neoplastic tissues. In normal tissues, claudin -3 was immunoexpressed in normal epithelia of intestine, kidney, liver, skin, lung, and in endothelia, as well as in the blood–brain barrier (Wolburg et al, 2003). Furthermore, Ibrahim et al (2007) detected immunohistochemical expression of claudins 1, 4, 5 and 7 in the human dental germ.
In Different Cancers:

Immunohistochemical expression of claudin-3 has been widely detected in many cancers. These studies have shown controversial results. Some studies showed up-regulation of claudin-3 in some tumors such as esophageal adenocarcinoma (Gyorffy et al, 2005), gastric adenocarinomas (Resnick et al, 2005) and metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (Soini et al, 2006). They concluded that claudin-3 might be a useful diagnostic biomarker or a therapeutic target for these cancers. On the contrary, many studies showed down-regulation of claudin-3 such as in colon ( Ersoz et al 2011), in breast (Szasz et al 2011), esophageal (lee et al 2012), and pancreatic carcinoma (Tsutsumi et al 2012).

Aro et al (2010) analyzed patterns of distribution and intensity of expression of claudins 1, 3, 4, and 7 in mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC) of salivary glands. Correlations between the expression of claudins, tumor grade, and survival were explored. In immunohistochemical analysis, they observed high claudin-3 expression in intermediate and high grade MEC, and low expression in low-grade MEC. They succeeded to use the intensity of claudin-3 to categorize tumors into grades in 71.8% of cases, correctly. However, no significant difference was achieved among the levels of claudin-3 in tumor grades and patient behavior. They concluded that analysis of staining intensities of claudin-3 could be useful as an auxiliary diagnostic and prognostic tool in patients with salivary gland MEC.

Lourenço et al (2010) employed a panel of anti-claudin antibodies against claudins 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 to map claudin expression in cases of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). They found that claudins were strongly present in well-differentiated tumors; they presented mild and low expression in moderately differentiated OSCC, and were negative in poorly differentiated OSCC. They added that claudin expression patterns showed a strong correlation with histological type of OSCC; its expression was decreased in areas of invasion, and negative in poorly differentiated tumors. They concluded that claudin-3 immunoexpression was associated with well differentiated tumors and good prognosis.

Many studies examined the expression of other claudins in oral cancer. Lourenço et al (2010) pointed out that lack of claudin-7 expression in OSCC might be used to identify patients with increased risk for regional recurrence. In 2012, Kunio et al suggested that loss of claudin-7 expression was associated closely with invasion and lymph metastasis and is an unfavorable prognostic factor in patients with OSCC. On the other hand, Carvalho et al (2010) observed increased claudin-1 expression with increase in the grade of oral dysplasia, this suggested the involvement of claudin-1 in the progression of this lesion. Moreover, De Aquino et al (2012) observed that metastatic tumors lip SCC exhibited higher expression of claudin-1 than nonmetastatic tumors. Their results suggested an important role of claudin-1 in the development of metastasis in lip SCCs.
In Different Odontogenic tumors

Although the expression of claudins was widely studied in different cancers, scarce studies were accomplished to study their expression in odontogenic lesions. For the best of our knowledge, only two studies were detected in the available literature studying the expression of different claudins in odontogenic cysts and tumors.

Ibrahim et al (2007) used the immunohistochemical expression to study the location of claudins 1, 4, 5 and 7 in benign and malignant ameloblastomas, in addition to human dental germ. They found that all cellular variants of benign solid ameloblastomas showed strong immunoreactivity for claudins 1 and 7. The most staining was concentrated in the loose polyhedral stellate reticulum-like central cells and particularly in the areas of squamous differentiation. On the contrary, Claudin 4 and 5 showed moderate and weak immunoreactivity for the central cells, respectively. Moreover, both of them showed negative immunoexpression for the peripheral cells of benign ameloblastomas. However, they showed that no significant differences in claudins' immunoexpression between benign and malignant ameloblastic tumors were observed. They pointed out that while the expression of the claudins 4 and 7 might be related to incipient cystic degeneration, claudin 1 expression was related to the areas of squamous differentiation.

Siar et al (2013) evaluated the immunohistochemical expression and localization of five tight junction proteins or claudins (1, 3, 4, 5, and 7) in the keratocystic odontogenic tumor (KCOT) and compared it with dentigerous cysts (DCs) and radicular cysts (RCs). Furthermore, they correlated their immunohistochemical expression with the biological behavior of the studied lesions. They observed marked claudin-3 loss of expression in KCOT basal layer compared with DCs and RCs. they suggested that claudin-3 downregulation might indicate altered or loss of basal cell polarity and impaired barrier function of KCOT lining epithelium. In contrast, they pointed out that the distribution patterns of claudins 1, 4, 5, and 7 were less distinctive; suggesting that these molecules probably play limited roles in influencing the different growth potentials of all the examined lesions. In Conclusion, their findings suggested that differential claudin expressions in the lining epithelium of KCOTs, DCs, and RCs probably reflect their neoplastic or nonneoplastic nature.
The aim of the present work is:
To determine the immunohistochemical expression of claudin 3 in radicular cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, unicystic ameloblastoma and ameloblastoma.
To compare the expression levels of claudin marker among the studied lesions
Finally, to correlate the obtained results with their biological behaviors.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
1-Specimen Selection:

A total of 40 cases of paraffin embedded tissue samples will be selected as follow: radicular cyst (10 cases), odontogenic keratocyst (10 cases), unicystic ameloblastoma (10 cases) and ameloblastoma (10 cases).
2-Immunohistochemical Reagents:
a. Monoclonal antibody against claudin -3.
b. An immunohistochemical universal kit.
For histopathological confirmation of diagnosis, paraffin blocks will be cut into 4um-thick, and stained with routine hematoxylin and eosin.
Parallel sections for immunohistochemical staining will be cut and placed on positively charged slides.
Immunohistochemistry will be performed using monoclonal antibodies against claudin -3.
Assessment of immunostaining will be performed by two methods:
Transmitted light microscope and computerized image analyzer.
All the obtained data from the computer image analysis will be tabulated and statistically evaluated.
